profiles.meeting_scenario: A brainstorming meeting between two ML systems researchers who are planning a survey-style workshop submission tentatively titled 'A Survey of Large-Scale Deep Learning Serving System Optimization: Challenges and Opportunities.' They have both skimmed a draft seed outline and are meeting to generate candidate angles for the survey's taxonomy, identify which recent serving techniques to group together, and decide what kind of contribution would make the survey feel publishable rather than merely descriptive. The agenda is to brainstorm: (1) what should count as the core organizing lens for 'large-scale' serving, (2) which families of optimization techniques belong in scope, and (3) what concrete deliverable they can aim to produce in the next two weeks. The expected outcome is a seemingly shared plan for an outline, a reading list, and a lightweight comparative artifact, even though several second-order assumptions remain misaligned.

members.name: Dr. Maya Srinivasan
members.expertise: Distributed inference systems, scheduling for GPU clusters, model serving architecture
members.background: Leads a university lab on large-scale ML infrastructure and previously spent four years at a cloud provider working on production inference platforms.
members.private_state: Wants the survey to be recognized as a systems-oriented piece that can seed a future NSF proposal, so she is quietly steering toward a taxonomy grounded in deployment architecture and operational bottlenecks rather than model-internal tricks.
hidden_assumptions: In a serving paper, 'large-scale' is primarily about fleet-level deployment conditions such as multi-tenant clusters, geographically distributed replicas, and sustained production traffic rather than merely the size of an individual model.

When people say 'serving system optimization,' they usually mean optimizations in the runtime, scheduler, placement layer, batching policy, memory orchestration, or cluster architecture, not modifications to the model weights or training pipeline.
A survey is 'publishable' if it offers a principled taxonomy and synthesizes disparate systems work into reusable design dimensions, even without a reproducible code artifact.

References to 'recent LLM serving work' naturally point to systems papers like vLLM, Orca, Sarathi-Serve, and related runtime/kernel or scheduler efforts, because those are the canonical exemplars in this space.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: LLM inference optimization, quantization, KV-cache compression, benchmark-driven evaluation
members.background: Works on efficient language model deployment and recently interned with an industry applied research team that built experimental LLM serving stacks for enterprise copilots.
members.private_state: Wants the project to produce a visible artifact that helps his job search, so he is quietly nudging the survey toward fast-moving LLM-serving techniques and a benchmark table or repository that can be cited independently.
hidden_assumptions: In current ML research conversation, 'large-scale' mostly means serving frontier or near-frontier models whose parameter count, context length, and KV-cache footprint dominate system behavior, even if deployment is on a limited number of nodes.

When people discuss 'serving optimization,' model-side inference accelerations such as quantization, speculative decoding, prefix caching, and attention sparsification are part of the serving stack because they materially change runtime cost.

A survey is only likely to gain traction if it includes a concrete comparative artifact such as a benchmark matrix, code repository, or reproducible experimental appendix rather than just conceptual categorization.

References to 'recent LLM serving work' naturally include papers and blogs on speculative decoding, paged attention variants, quantized inference, and continuous batching implementations, regardless of whether they are framed as systems papers.
If no one explicitly excludes industry artifacts, it is reasonable to treat major open-source implementations and engineering blog posts as first-class evidence alongside peer-reviewed papers.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly say the survey should focus on 'large-scale deep learning serving systems.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means fleet-scale production serving: many replicas, multi-tenancy, autoscaling, scheduling, heterogeneous accelerators, and operational constraints across a serving platform.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means very large-model inference: huge parameter counts, long contexts, KV-cache pressure, and runtime challenges driven by model size even in relatively small deployments.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase appears uncontroversial because both can cite LLM serving examples and both are genuinely talking about real scale phenomena, so surface agreement on 'large-scale' masks different axes of scale.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to organize the survey around 'serving optimizations' and to separate categories within the 'serving stack.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the serving stack starts after a trained model artifact exists, so the survey should emphasize request routing, batching, placement, runtime memory management, kernel scheduling, and deployment topology; quantization only belongs if treated as a runtime systems choice already packaged for deployment.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes any technique that reduces online inference cost is in scope, including quantization, speculative decoding, pruning-for-serving, cache reuse schemes, and model-architecture-aware accelerations.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use broad systems language like 'end-to-end latency' and 'inference efficiency,' which naturally covers both runtime and model-side optimizations without forcing an explicit boundary discussion.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They say the paper needs a 'strong contribution' or has to feel 'publishable' rather than a generic summary.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes publishability comes from a crisp taxonomy, a synthesis of bottleneck patterns, and a forward-looking research agenda that unifies systems subareas.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes publishability requires some concrete comparative artifact, such as a benchmarked table, open repository, or reproducible matrix of serving techniques, even if the taxonomy is good.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both endorse the same high-level goal of making the survey substantive, and in brainstorming meetings people often intentionally leave 'contribution' underspecified because multiple forms of value seem compatible.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'recent serving papers' are the anchor set
misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to 'the recent serving papers everyone cites' and 'the 2023-2024 LLM serving work' as if they have the same anchor literature in mind.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking primarily of peer-reviewed systems papers and a few well-established runtimes such as vLLM, Orca, Sarathi-Serve, DistServe, and cluster scheduling work.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of a broader anchor set that mixes peer-reviewed papers with influential open-source systems, engineering blog posts, speculative decoding papers, quantization papers, and rapidly adopted repos.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both can casually name overlapping examples like vLLM, which creates enough common ground that neither notices the other is using a different inclusion rule for the surrounding literature.

turns.inner_thought: I want to anchor this as a systems survey, not let it drift into a grab bag of model tricks. If we frame it around large-scale deep learning serving systems, I can steer toward deployment architecture, scheduling, batching, placement, memory orchestration, and operational bottlenecks across production platforms. For publishability, the key is a clean taxonomy with reusable design dimensions and a research agenda, not a giant artifact chase.
turns.utterance: Maybe the most useful way to start is to make sure we're framing the main challenges in large-scale deep learning serving systems, and then leave today with a really clean organizing taxonomy. If we can get that right, the rest of the survey will feel much more coherent.
